assignment: Your principal has decided that all students must participate in at least one extracurricular activity. For example, students could participate in sports, work on the yearbook, or serve on the student council. Do you agree or disagree with this decision? Use specific details and examples to convince others to support your position.
essay_1:
One Activity Is Not Too Much

When I first heard our principal wants every student to join at least one extracurricular activity, I was kind of mad. I already have homework and chores and on Thursdays I have to watch my little brother. But then I thought about it some more and I changed my mind. I agree with the principal, but only if the rule is flexible for kids who need it to be.

My first reason is that alot of kids don't know what they like until somebody makes them try it. Last year my friend Marcus joined yearbook only because his mom made him. He complained about it for like two weeks straight. Then by October he was staying after school to fix the photo pages and now he says he wants to do graphic design when he grows up. He never would of found that out if he just went home at 3:00 and played video games. Some kids are quiet or not sure of themselfs, so a rule like this gives them a push.

Another reason is activities teach you stuff that classes don't. If I mess up in math it only hurts my grade. But if I skip soccer practice the whole team has to deal with it, and my coach makes sure I know it. Also the kids on student council have to listen to everybody complain about the lunch food and then they have to actually plan things with real money. Adults have to do things like that all the time and you can't learn it from a worksheet.

It also helps you meet people. Our school has around nine hundred kids, and you can go all three years only knowing the people in your classes. In a club there are kids from different grades and different friend groups. A sixth grader in chess club might play against an eighth grader, and then the hallway isn't so scary anymore. I think when kids feel like they belong somewhere they come to school more and they get in less trouble too.

I know some people are going to disagree with me. Some students have jobs or a really long bus ride, or they have to help out their family, and some kids are just shy. Those are good points. That is why the rule shouldn't be too strict. The school should have clubs that meet during lunch or advisory so nobody has to miss the bus. Small things should count too, like helping in the library once a week. And if a student really can't do anything at all, they should be able to go talk to a counselor and get excused.

In conclusion, one activity is not that much to ask for. It is only an hour or two a week and you could get a new skill or a new friend out of it. Most of us would not sign up on our own, so I think the principal is right.
essay_2:
One Activity Is Not Too Much to Ask

When I first heard that our principal wants every student to join at least one activity after school, I groaned. I already have homework, chores, and a little brother I have to watch on Thursdays. To me it sounded like a terrible, unfair, annoying rule. Then I thought about it for a while and changed my mind. I agree with the principal, as long as the rule has some room in it.

The biggest reason is that kids find out what they like when somebody makes them try it. Last year my friend Marcus signed up for yearbook because his mom made him. He was angry, he complained and whined for two weeks, and he called it boring, stupid, and a waste. By October he was staying late to fix the photo pages. Now he says he wants to study graphic design. Without his mom he would have gone home at 3:00 and played video games.

Activities also teach you things that classes leave out. In math, if I mess up, it only goes on my grade. On the soccer team, if I skip practice, ten other people have to do my part. Kids on student council have to listen to angry complaints about the awful, gross lunch menu. They still have to plan something with a budget. Adults do that every day. A worksheet is only a piece of paper.

There is a reason with friends too. Our school has about nine hundred students. You can go three years and only know the people in your classes. That is lonely, sad, and kind of scary. A club mixes the grades up, and it is fun, friendly, and a great way to laugh with new people. A sixth grader in chess club sits across from an eighth grader. After that the hallway is a different place.

I know what people will say against this. Some kids have jobs, long bus rides, or have to help at home, and some are shy. So the school should have clubs that meet at lunch or in advisory. It should count small things, like helping in the library once a week. A student who has a serious problem at home should be able to talk to a counselor and get out of it.

With those changes, one activity is an hour or two a week. Most of us will stay home unless somebody pushes us. We are lazy, scared of looking dumb, and worried that everybody will ignore us. I was afraid of that in sixth grade. I sat in my room every afternoon that whole year. The principal is right, and I am glad about the rule. I only wish I had been pushed when I was eleven, because I think I would have loved having a team and good friends.
